So, it has been observed for former evening, that the expenses of our establishments, with the addition of the interest of the National debt, amount to more than the whole rental of the kingdom; and it might be added that the kingdom were to get so far as to be sufficient to bear existing national debt. Blessed indeed.

In the same relation, the Earl of Bathurst was far from noting the agricultural distresses, but contented that similar distresses had always occurred in termination of a war.

The Earl Carnarvon declared, that what were called cultural distresses, were in fact general successes, embracing every class and description of the community.

Sensitive; but one of the strongest we have seen is that of Mr. Preston, member of parliament, and whilst most loyal admirer of it, an advocate of the law, and one of those martial gentlemen who toss up their caps with loudest plaudits to the glory of Old England.

Save come of the features of this glory, fresh in the face of her warmest admirers. So we look around us at the present moment, and view the distresses in which the country is involved, from the inability of a large part of the population to answer the demands of government; whoever examines the great change which has taken place in the condition of large part of the community, hurled from wealth to poverty; from influence to distress; whoever enquires into the fact, and finds that a very considerable part of the people are deprived by means of legal process; whoever finds the fact is, the poor are increasing daily in number, while the ability of the persons, who are liable to contribute to their maintenance, is diminished.

Observation-Disclosures shall show the fact is, that a large part of the community are in want of employment though willing to labour, and that their former employers, unable to afford to pay, their wages, are even so to be met with in different parishes asking for employment, and urging the interest of the former to pay them for actual labour than to pay them in rates of idleness from the poor rate; while the farmer, though convinced of the justice of the appeal, is unable to meet this appeal; his interest further that a large portion of that industrious part of the community, the little farmers (the favourites of the ancient system) with their large families (the best hope of the state and most valuable part of the community) are ceasing to be farmers from necessity, and becoming pensioners to the poor rate; while in some townships, the persons who formerly contributed to the poor, appealing for relief on the ground of their own poverty, and numbers of them obliged to abandon the cultivation of their farms, are become burdens on those parts of the parish which alone are cultivated, thus taxing the industry of their neighbours, and fastening them to the same entire nifty of extreme indigence.

We must admit that there is something wrong in the system, and that it is, and not the spirit of complaint and dissension, imposes the duty of examining into these evils, that they may be understood and fairly met. The person who supposes this picture to be overcharged, will find himself mistaken. In some places, says the same writer, the lands actually deserted, and growing no other crop than weeds, &c. By means of a restriction on the circulating medium, a total inability to purchase exists and a value deprecated by the reduction of the rental, is still further depressed by the competition to sell; and who is benefited by this sudden, extraordinary and unexpected change? No one besides the creditors, who can realize their money, and not few are they.

The present unfortunate state of the country presents the most lamentable history of Government, excessive taxes, and for balances in the hands of receivers, &c., &c., many of them receivers, are thus called on to day the deposits with which they again call on their debtors; and the receivers using the harsh process of extents and mortgages are depriving their securities from the difficulty of obtaining interest; and, as to Bankers, from the necessity of having ready money, and needy improvident landlords, levying their rents by distress. What wretched and melancholy picture!

If such be the general condition of the Empire, how much more deplorable is that of Ireland! What gallant and generous country has ever entailed so constant a struggle! Three-fourths of her people are denied the right of worshipping their God according to the dictates of their consciences, or compelled to contribute to the maintenance of the pampered and privileged priesthood of another sect. Ireland is not to be correlated by successes, which she has right to demand, but compelled to obey the regulations of an unjust taskmaster. Even the Irish troops are to be stationed on her fields, to keep her in subjection, and to gather the fruits of their industry in tithes and in taxes. Is any wonder, that her high-minded sons are seeking from those green fields to be laid chiefly.

We shall get, however, a better view of the state of the Empire, by narrowing down our enquiries to the single point it is the one which now engrosses all her attention—we mean, her revenue.

In one of the former Nos. of this paper, we expatiated on this topic attempting to shew the embarrassments to which her revenue was reduced.
